title: How Did a 0.5 mm Animal Survive Space? 🐻
description:
How did a tardigrade, the half-millimeter water bear, survive 10 days in open space? It dries itself into a glassy 'tun' and switches its body off.

Follow Zorbly for a new mystery every day.

#shorts #tardigrade #animalfacts #science
pinned_comment: Be honest: how long do you think YOU would last in space without a suit?
topic: How did a tardigrade survive 10 days in open space? (dries into a tun, proteins vitrify cells, metabolism stops; FOTON-M3 2007, most revived within 30 min; ~1000x radiation tolerance)
script:
You'd pass out in 15 seconds in space.
How did this animal last 10 days?
Meet the tardigrade, or water bear,
half a millimeter long, with eight chubby legs.
When its home dries out,
it pulls in its legs,
squeezes out almost all its water,
and curls into a tiny ball called a tun.
Inside, special proteins set like glass,
holding every cell in place,
and its body switches off.
In 2007, scientists flew dried tardigrades into orbit.
Back on Earth, they added water,
and most woke up within half an hour.
They can take a thousand times more radiation than you.
So how long would you last up there?
key_facts: In 2007 (FOTON-M3, ESA TARDIS/TARSE) dehydrated tardigrades spent 10 days exposed to open space; >68% of UV-shielded ones revived within 30 minutes of rehydration and many produced viable embryos (Wikipedia: Tardigrades in space; ESA)

In the tun (cryptobiosis) state they retract legs, lose almost all body water and metabolism is suspended; disordered proteins may form a glass-like matrix protecting cells (Wikipedia: Environmental tolerance in tardigrades)
Tardigrades withstand ~1,000x more radiation than other animals: median lethal ~5,000 Gy vs 5-10 Gy fatal for humans
Tardigrades are about 0.5 mm long with eight legs
Unprotected humans in vacuum lose consciousness in about 15 seconds (Space.com / NASA)
